lines.text: Does everyone need the same food in the same amounts?
Clearly not. A twelve-year-old is still growing and needs more protein for her size
than her grandfatber does. A farmhand doing heavy work all day needs more
energy than someone at a desk. A person recovering from illness has different
needs again. Requirements shift with age, sex, level of physical activity, state of
A balanced diet is one that supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in
the right amounts, together with enough roughage and water. Note the phrase
a particular person. There is no single balanced diet for everybody — the idea
only means anything once you say who is eating.
Go back to your food diary in Table 3.1.
Against each day, mark which of the five nutrients that day's food supplied.
2. Find the nutrient that is missing or thin most often.
3. Name two foods, available near you and affordable, that would fill the gap.
4. Do not redesign your whole diet. Change one thing, and keep it.
Two snacks, both sold in a packet. Compare what is printed on them.
The wafers carry half again as much energy, five times the fat, roughly a third of
the protein and under a third of the fibre. On the numbers, the chana is the better
food by a wide margin — and it usually costs less.
Foods high in sugar and fat but low in protein, vitamins, minerals and flbre are
called junk foods: wafers, candy bars, carbonated drinks and much else sold as
a snack. They deliver energy and little else. Eaten often, they crowd better food
off the plate and lead to weight gain and the health problems that follow.
